passage.title: Excerpt from "The Cart That Changed the Supermarket"

lines.text: Priscilla Vance writes about the history of everyday consumer objects for a retail-industry newsletter. The following is adapted from her article on the invention of the folding shopping cart.
Excerpt from "The Cart That Changed the Supermarket"
by Priscilla Vance

lines.html: For most of the history of grocery shopping, customers carried their purchases in a handbasket, and a handbasket has a stubborn limit: at some point it gets too heavy to lift. In 1936, a grocery store owner in Oklahoma City named Sylvan Goldman noticed that his customers stopped shopping the moment their basket filled up, no matter how many bargains still lined the shelves. A full basket, he realized, was not a sign that a customer was satisfied. It was a sign that the store had stopped selling to them for the day.
lines.text: For most of the history of grocery shopping, customers carried their purchases in a handbasket, and a handbasket has a stubborn limit: at some point it gets too heavy to lift. In 1936, a grocery store owner in Oklahoma City named Sylvan Goldman noticed that his customers stopped shopping the moment their basket filled up, no matter how many bargains still lined the shelves. A full basket, he realized, was not a sign that a customer was satisfied. It was a sign that the store had stopped selling to them for the day.

lines.html: Goldman's solution grew out of an ordinary folding chair. Late one evening in his office, he looked at a wooden folding chair and pictured a metal frame built the same way: two baskets stacked on a wheeled frame that folded flat for storage, one basket at seat height and a smaller one below it. He sketched the idea, hired a mechanic named Fred Young to build a working model, and by June of 1937 had a small fleet of the carts, which he called "folding basket carriers," rolling on the floor of his Humpty Dumpty supermarket chain.
lines.text: Goldman's solution grew out of an ordinary folding chair. Late one evening in his office, he looked at a wooden folding chair and pictured a metal frame built the same way: two baskets stacked on a wheeled frame that folded flat for storage, one basket at seat height and a smaller one below it. He sketched the idea, hired a mechanic named Fred Young to build a working model, and by June of 1937 had a small fleet of the carts, which he called "folding basket carriers," rolling on the floor of his Humpty Dumpty supermarket chain.

lines.html: The invention should have sold itself. It did not. Male customers found the carts undignified, comparing them to baby carriages. Female customers, according to Goldman's later recollections, associated the carts with the perception that they could not physically manage a shopping basket themselves, an idea some considered insulting. Store employees pushed carts toward customers at the entrance, only to watch shoppers set their handbaskets down inside the cart's basket and abandon the cart itself at the first aisle.
lines.text: The invention should have sold itself. It did not. Male customers found the carts undignified, comparing them to baby carriages. Female customers, according to Goldman's later recollections, associated the carts with the perception that they could not physically manage a shopping basket themselves, an idea some considered insulting. Store employees pushed carts toward customers at the entrance, only to watch shoppers set their handbaskets down inside the cart's basket and abandon the cart itself at the first aisle.

lines.html: Goldman's response was distinctly theatrical. He hired men and women, paying them by the hour, to walk through his stores pushing the new carts as though they were ordinary customers, filling them with groceries and chatting amiably near the entrance where new arrivals could see them. He also stationed a greeter at the door whose entire job was to hand a cart to every shopper, whether they wanted one or not, and to explain, cheerfully, that it was simply the way the store now worked. Within a few weeks, the artificial familiarity had become real familiarity, and shoppers began pushing the carts themselves.

He also stationed a greeter at the door whose entire job was to hand a cart to every shopper, whether they wanted one or not, and to explain, cheerfully, that it was simply the way the store now worked. Within a few weeks, the artificial familiarity had become real familiarity, and shoppers began pushing the carts themselves.

lines.html: The commercial effect surprised even Goldman. Once a customer had a cart large enough to hold far more than a handbasket, the practical ceiling on a single shopping trip disappeared, and the average amount a customer spent per visit began to climb. Competing grocers who had initially dismissed the carts as an unnecessary expense installed fleets of their own within a few years, once the sales figures from stores that had adopted them became difficult to argue with.

Competing grocers who had initially dismissed the carts as an unnecessary expense installed fleets of their own within a few years, once the sales figures from stores that had adopted them became difficult to argue with.

lines.html: Goldman patented his design and later refined it further, adding a hinged back panel that let one cart's frame nest inside another's, which solved the considerable problem of where to store dozens of bulky carts overnight. He founded a company to manufacture and sell the carts to other grocery chains and became a wealthy man from an invention that, by his own account, nearly failed for want of anyone willing to be seen pushing one.

He founded a company to manufacture and sell the carts to other grocery chains and became a wealthy man from an invention that, by his own account, nearly failed for want of anyone willing to be seen pushing one.

lines.html: Later interviews with Goldman preserved a detail he seems to have found quietly satisfying: the same carts that shoppers had once refused to touch became, within a decade, so essential to the ordinary experience of a grocery store that almost no one arriving at the entrance thought to ask why one was there at all. The convenience had become invisible, which is generally what happens to a good invention once people stop noticing it was ever new.

The convenience had become invisible, which is generally what happens to a good invention once people stop noticing it was ever new.

lines.html: Grocery historians who study the episode tend to draw a broader lesson from it than the cart itself. The technical problem, a wheeled frame, was simple enough that any competent mechanic could have solved it in an afternoon. The harder problem was a matter of habit and self-image: shoppers had to be persuaded, gradually and somewhat indirectly, that pushing a cart said nothing about how capable they were of carrying their own groceries. Goldman's paid decoys were, in effect, an early experiment in changing a social habit by making a new behavior look ordinary before it actually was, a strategy since borrowed by marketers selling products with no relation to groceries at all.

directions.subject: English Language Arts
directions.title: READING COMPREHENSION

passage.title: Excerpt from "The Neighborhood Next Door Is Hotter Than Yours"

lines.text: Dr. Camille Iversen is an environmental scientist who studies urban climate patterns. The following is adapted from her article on the urban heat island effect.
Excerpt from "The Neighborhood Next Door Is Hotter Than Yours"
by Dr. Camille Iversen

lines.html: On a July afternoon when the official forecast reads ninety-two degrees, a single city can quietly contain half a dozen different climates. A dashboard thermometer crossing from a leafy residential street into a treeless commercial strip can climb several degrees in the space of a few blocks, without a cloud moving and without the sun getting any closer. Researchers who study this pattern call it the urban heat island effect, and one of the clearest predictors of how badly a given neighborhood suffers from it turns out to be a number city planners rarely mentioned until recently: the percentage of that neighborhood covered by tree canopy.
lines.text: On a July afternoon when the official forecast reads ninety-two degrees, a single city can quietly contain half a dozen different climates. A dashboard thermometer crossing from a leafy residential street into a treeless commercial strip can climb several degrees in the space of a few blocks, without a cloud moving and without the sun getting any closer. Researchers who study this pattern call it the urban heat island effect, and one of the clearest predictors of how badly a given neighborhood suffers from it turns out to be a number city planners rarely mentioned until recently: the percentage of that neighborhood covered by tree canopy.

lines.html: The physical mechanism is straightforward once it is spelled out. Pavement, roofing, and dark building materials absorb solar radiation efficiently and release it back as heat throughout the afternoon and evening, a process scientists call thermal mass. A mature tree canopy interrupts that cycle in two ways at once: its leaves intercept sunlight before it ever strikes the pavement below, and the tree continuously releases water vapor through its leaves in a cooling process called transpiration, which lowers the surrounding air temperature the way sweat cools skin. A block with dense tree cover is, in effect, running its own modest air-conditioning system for free, all day, without anyone flipping a switch.
lines.text: The physical mechanism is straightforward once it is spelled out. Pavement, roofing, and dark building materials absorb solar radiation efficiently and release it back as heat throughout the afternoon and evening, a process scientists call thermal mass. A mature tree canopy interrupts that cycle in two ways at once: its leaves intercept sunlight before it ever strikes the pavement below, and the tree continuously releases water vapor through its leaves in a cooling process called transpiration, which lowers the surrounding air temperature the way sweat cools skin. A block with dense tree cover is, in effect, running its own modest air-conditioning system for free, all day, without anyone flipping a switch.

lines.html: A research team studying temperature variation across one mid-sized city set out to measure how much difference canopy coverage actually made, rather than assume it from the general mechanism. Volunteers mounted temperature sensors on bicycles and rode fixed routes through six neighborhoods at the same hour on the same clear afternoon, chosen specifically to eliminate weather as a variable. Each neighborhood's canopy coverage had already been mapped separately using aerial imagery, so the team could compare temperature readings against a percentage figure for each area rather than a vague impression of "leafy" versus "not leafy."
lines.text: A research team studying temperature variation across one mid-sized city set out to measure how much difference canopy coverage actually made, rather than assume it from the general mechanism. Volunteers mounted temperature sensors on bicycles and rode fixed routes through six neighborhoods at the same hour on the same clear afternoon, chosen specifically to eliminate weather as a variable. Each neighborhood's canopy coverage had already been mapped separately using aerial imagery, so the team could compare temperature readings against a percentage figure for each area rather than a vague impression of "leafy" versus "not leafy."

lines.html: The results, summarized in the accompanying figure, showed a relationship too consistent to dismiss as coincidence. The neighborhood with the lowest canopy coverage recorded the highest average afternoon temperature of the six studied, while the neighborhood with the highest canopy coverage recorded the lowest, with the other four neighborhoods falling in between in almost the same order as their canopy percentages. The gap between the hottest and coolest neighborhoods that afternoon was large enough that a resident walking between them would notice it directly, without needing a thermometer to confirm what their own skin was already telling them.
lines.text: The results, summarized in the accompanying figure, showed a relationship too consistent to dismiss as coincidence. The neighborhood with the lowest canopy coverage recorded the highest average afternoon temperature of the six studied, while the neighborhood with the highest canopy coverage recorded the lowest, with the other four neighborhoods falling in between in almost the same order as their canopy percentages. The gap between the hottest and coolest neighborhoods that afternoon was large enough that a resident walking between them would notice it directly, without needing a thermometer to confirm what their own skin was already telling them.

lines.html: What surprised the research team was not that trees cooled their surroundings, which nobody seriously doubted going in, but how unevenly canopy coverage happened to be distributed across the city to begin with. The neighborhoods with the thinnest canopy were, disproportionately, the same neighborhoods with older industrial zoning, narrower residential lots, and fewer public parks, a pattern the team traced back to decisions about street width and lot planning made decades earlier, long before anyone involved in those decisions had heard the term urban heat island.

The neighborhoods with the thinnest canopy were, disproportionately, the same neighborhoods with older industrial zoning, narrower residential lots, and fewer public parks, a pattern the team traced back to decisions about street width and lot planning made decades earlier, long before anyone involved in those decisions had heard the term urban heat island.

lines.html: The consequences of that historical unevenness are not evenly distributed either. Higher afternoon and evening temperatures translate directly into higher electricity demand for air conditioning, which falls hardest on residents who can least afford a larger utility bill, and into greater heat-related health risk for anyone without reliable indoor cooling. A canopy gap that traces back to a decision made generations ago about how densely to build a neighborhood turns out to still be measurable in a modern resident's monthly bills and their risk during a heat wave, which is a much longer reach for an old zoning map than most people would expect.

A canopy gap that traces back to a decision made generations ago about how densely to build a neighborhood turns out to still be measurable in a modern resident's monthly bills and their risk during a heat wave, which is a much longer reach for an old zoning map than most people would expect.

lines.html: Several cities that have reviewed findings like these have begun treating tree planting less as a beautification project and more as a piece of infrastructure, budgeted and tracked the way a city tracks sewer lines or streetlights. Some now require a minimum canopy percentage for new residential developments, and a few have begun prioritizing new plantings specifically in the neighborhoods that measured hottest, rather than distributing new trees evenly across a city regardless of existing coverage. Advocates of this approach argue that an evenly distributed number of new trees, spread without regard for where the gaps already are, does little to close the specific gap that the temperature data revealed.

Advocates of this approach argue that an evenly distributed number of new trees, spread without regard for where the gaps already are, does little to close the specific gap that the temperature data revealed.

lines.html: None of this makes a single newly planted tree an instant fix. A young sapling provides only a fraction of the shade and transpiration of the mature canopy that produced the readings described above, and that canopy took decades to grow. What the temperature data does offer is a more precise account of where the investment should go first, replacing the old assumption that shade was simply a pleasant extra with the more exact finding that its absence carries a measurable, mappable cost.
